title: Minimum-Cost Robust Evidence Certificates for Horn Reasoning under Correlated Source Failures

paper.title: Minimum-Cost Robust Evidence Certificates for Horn Reasoning under Correlated Source Failures
paper.abstract: Abstract A small justification for a rule-based conclusion may disappear when a source is withdrawn, and multiple derivations need not provide independent evidence. We study minimum-cost certificates that preserve a Horn conclusion under every withdrawal of at most k k source domains. Evidence records remain distinct from asserted facts, supporting replicated attestations and overlapping failure dependencies. Transversals of minimal-support footprints characterize robustness and explain why disjoint-proof requirements can reject valid certificates. An exact procedure alternates weighted evidence selection with a source-failure oracle. A rule-closed counterinterpretation yields a globally valid selection cut without enumerating supports or failure scenarios. We prove correctness, finite termination, and cost optimality, establish coNP-completeness of unrestricted verification and NP-completeness of synthesis for every fixed budget, and identify a tractable reachability restriction. Experiments on controlled benchmarks, reachability graphs, and ontology-derived instances demonstrate that our counterinterpretation-guided synthesis achieves up to 92% optimum coverage within practical resource bounds, outperforming scenario expansion and general abduction while confirming the necessity of transversal-based reasoning over proof-packing heuristics.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Rule-based decisions often require premises that can be inspected, retained, or communicated. A release policy may combine signed test reports and attestations; a knowledge graph may infer relationships from several institutions’ records. Efficient materialization computes conclusions ( Motik et al. 2014 ) , while explanation and provenance expose their dependencies. When a provider becomes unavailable or is removed from an audit, the practical question is whether the retained evidence can still justify the decision. An inclusion-minimal explanation removes unnecessary premises, and a minimum-cost explanation reduces inspection or disclosure cost. Neither protects against withdrawal of its own premises: one cheap support may concentrate the entire justification in a single supplier. Retaining the full knowledge base can preserve alternatives but exceed an audit budget. We therefore select a fixed evidence package before failures occur and allow its successful derivation to change afterward. The quantifier order is evidence selection, universal source withdrawal, and existence of a surviving justification. Recovery uses only the selected records, as required by an archived audit package; it does not depend on later evidence acquisition. Counting proofs does not resolve this problem. Different derivations may reuse a record or depend on services within one failure domain. Conversely, requiring domain-disjoint proofs can reject evidence that survives every admissible withdrawal. Robustness depends on whether failed domains intersect all supports, not on whether supports can be packed without overlap. Example 1 (Release authorization). Authorization requires any two of checks a , b , c a,b,c , whose records depend on domains s A , s B , s C s_{A},s_{B},s_{C} . Retaining all three survives any single-domain withdrawal because any two suffice, yet their support footprints { s A , s B } \{s_{A},s_{B}\} , { s A , s C } \{s_{A},s_{C}\} , and { s B , s C } \{s_{B},s_{C}\} share domains pairwise, precluding disjoint proofs. An alternative attestation d d independently authorizes release at higher cost. Optimal robust certification must navigate both inspection costs and failure dependencies. While why-provenance ( Buneman et al. 2001 ) , semiring provenance ( Green et al. 2007 ) , and circuit representations ( Deutch et al. 2014 ) expose derivation dependencies, they do not select cost-optimal subsets resilient to source loss. Database resilience ( Freire et al. 2015 ) and Datalog deletion causality ( Thapa and Staab 2026 ) analyze answer vulnerability to tuple removals via minimal supports, but do not address ex-ante evidence synthesis under grouped, correlated domain withdrawals. Similarly, abduction-based explanations ( Ignatiev et al. 2019 ) , robust perturbation models ( La Malfa et al. 2021 ) , and lineage-driven fault injection ( Alvaro et al. 2015 ) seek explanations or fault witnesses without synthesizing minimum-cost packages resilient to source loss. We turn this support–transversal principle into a cost-sensitive separation framework specialized for correlated source domains. Our synthesis method alternates an exact weighted hitting-set master with an adversarial oracle. A defeating withdrawal yields a rule-closed counterinterpretation and a positive clause that every robust selection must satisfy. This uses established implicit hitting-set separation ( Saikko et al. 2016 ; Davies and Bacchus 2011 ) , with globally valid record cuts for shared failures. Horn closure handles recursive rules without admitting unsupported cycles as proofs. Our contributions are: (1) a record-level certification objective capturing correlated source failures; (2) a footprint characterization proving why proof packing is incomplete; (3) an exact synthesis algorithm with finite termination and cost optimality guarantees; (4) complexity results showing coNP-complete verification and NP-complete synthesis for fixed budgets; (5) a polynomial flow reduction for independent reachability; and (6) empirical evaluations demonstrating up to 92% optimum coverage and the necessity of cut strengthening over proof packing.

sections.heading: Relation to provenance and abduction
sections.text: Unlike recursive semiring provenance ( Bourgaux et al. 2022 ) or why-provenance enumeration ( Calautti et al. 2024b ; Calautti et al. 2024a ) , which face exponential compilation blowup ( Darwiche and Marquis 2002 ) , we target polynomial Boolean entailment under retained subsets. Query causality ( Meliou et al. 2010 ) and database resilience ( Freire et al. 2015 ) study individual tuple deletions rather than adversarial domain withdrawals. While Horn abduction ( Kakas et al. 1992 ) , sufficient reasons ( Darwiche and Hirth 2020 ) , and diagnosis ( Reiter 1987 ) select static premises, they do not guarantee survival against subsequent failures; and unlike minimum label cuts ( Zhang and Tang 2020 ) , Horn conjunctions preclude graph reductions.

Use vertex atoms r v r_{v} , edge atoms g u ​ v g_{uv} , the sole trusted fact r s r_{s} , and precisely the rules r v ← r u , g u ​ v r_{v}\leftarrow r_{u},g_{uv} . Each edge has one record asserting g u ​ v g_{uv} ; the target is r t r_{t} . Minimum-cost k k -robust certification is solvable by a minimum-cost flow of value k + 1 k+1 with unit edge capacities. Infeasible flow implies infeasible certification. Proof. By the max-flow/min-cut theorem, a subgraph survives all ≤ k \leq k edge deletions iff it contains k + 1 k+1 edge-disjoint s s – t t paths. A minimum-cost integral unit flow of value k + 1 k+1 identifies an optimal cycle-free edge subset, which directly defines an optimal k k -robust certificate. □ \square When a source labels multiple edges or rules require joint premises, path formulations miss correlated cuts, but Algorithm 1 remains exact.

Knowledge-base benchmarks use positive Horn translations of Lehigh University Benchmark ( Guo et al. 2005 ) data (LUBM-1 and LUBM-5), mapping domains to institutions and data pipelines. Targets are sampled across shallow and recursive derivations with backward rule slicing; replicated assertions receive distinct record identities with shared or separate dependencies.

sections.heading: Implementation, metrics, and ablations
sections.text: Our framework is implemented in Python 3.11 using PySAT ( Ignatiev et al. 2018 ) , combining RC2 for the master with Glucose 4.1 and Sinz’s cardinality encoding ( Sinz 2005 ) for the oracle. All experiments were conducted single-threaded on AMD EPYC 7742 processors (2.25 GHz) running Ubuntu 22.04, with a 600 s timeout and 8 GiB memory limit. Primary metrics include feasible cost, certified optimum coverage, proven infeasibility, runtime, and memory. The price of robustness is measured by premium ⁡ ( k ) = cost ⁡ ( C k ∗ ) − cost ⁡ ( C 0 ∗ ) cost ⁡ ( C 0 ∗ ) , \operatorname{premium}(k)=\frac{\operatorname{cost}(C_{k}^{*})-\operatorname{cost}(C_{0}^{*})}{\operatorname{cost}(C_{0}^{*})}, (13) where C k ∗ C_{k}^{*} and C 0 ∗ C_{0}^{*} denote certified robust and nominal optima, respectively. Targets derivable solely from trusted facts require zero nominal cost and are reported separately.

sections.heading: Scalability and runtime dynamics.
sections.text: As shown in Table 1 and Figure 2 (a), Algorithm 1 scales gracefully across both synthetic Horn systems and knowledge bases, achieving up to 92% optimum coverage. In contrast, explicit scenario synthesis suffers severe combinatorial explosion ( O ⁡ ( ( m + 1 ) k ​ L ) O((m+1)^{k}L) ), rapidly timing out and exhausting memory for k ≥ 2 k\geq 2 . Compiled abduction and provenance compilation avoid full unrolling but stall on large or recursive instances due to circuit blowup and lack of source-aware cuts. On all mutually solved instances, all exact solvers yield identical optimal costs, confirming empirical correctness.

sections.heading: Incompleteness of proof packing.
sections.text: Domain-disjoint proof packing exhibits a severe false-negative rate, resolving under a third of benchmark instances due to overlapping support footprints (generalizing Example 2). Even when disjoint supports exist, enforcing strict disjointness over-restricts search and inflates costs, confirming Proposition 1: disjoint packing cannot substitute for transversal reasoning.

sections.heading: Exact ground-truth calibration.
sections.text: On reachability instances with unique edge domains, Proposition 5 equates robust certification to minimum-cost unit-capacity flow of value k + 1 k+1 . Across all 80 topologies, Algorithm 1 achieves 100% agreement with the polynomial flow optimum. Under correlated failures, min-cost flow becomes unsound, whereas Algorithm 1 continues to synthesize verified optima.

sections.heading: Robustness premium and greedy repair.
sections.text: Evaluating Equation ( 13 ) demonstrates that securing conclusions against correlated withdrawals requires substantial cost premiums as k k increases; nominal solutions ( k = 0 k=0 ) fail checks in > 95 % >95\% of cases. Greedy repair accumulates redundant records, producing uncompetitive certificates far costlier than certified optima.

sections.heading: Ablation analysis (Table 2 ).
sections.text: Table 2 isolates each component’s contribution on controlled Horn instances ( | ℰ | ≤ 512 , k = 2 |\mathcal{E}|\leq 512,k=2 ). Cut strengthening cuts master calls by 37% and yields cuts under half the length of raw witnesses, reducing total runtime by 29% with negligible closure overhead. Candidate exclusion thrashes severely. Dominance pruning eliminates redundant duplicate records upfront, while relevance slicing halves oracle verification time.

sections.heading: Sensitivity and error analysis
sections.text: Denser source overlap requires more master-oracle iterations but maintains stable memory. Wider rule bodies scale linearly in oracle check time, while log-normal costs accelerate master search through aggressive pruning.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: We presented an exact framework for synthesizing minimum-cost evidence certificates for Horn reasoning under correlated source failures. By separating record selection from asserted facts, our footprint characterization explains why proof packing is incomplete, while closed counterinterpretations yield globally valid cuts that bypass exponential scenario unrolling. We established finite termination, cost optimality, tight complexity bounds, and a tractable flow restriction. Experiments confirm that our method resolves up to 92% of benchmarks, outperforming scenario expansion and general abduction. Future work includes multiquery cut reuse, structured withdrawal constraints, and non-additive costs.

We study minimum-cost certificates that preserve a Horn conclusion under every withdrawal of at most k k source domains. Evidence records remain distinct from asserted facts, supporting replicated attestations and overlapping failure dependencies. Transversals of minimal-support footprints characterize robustness and explain why disjoint-proof requirements can reject valid certificates. An exact procedure alternates weighted evidence selection with a source-failure oracle. A rule-closed counterinterpretation yields a globally valid selection cut without enumerating supports or failure scenarios. We prove correctness, finite termination, and cost optimality, establish coNP-completeness of unrestricted verification and NP-completeness of synthesis for every fixed budget, and identify a tractable reachability restriction. Experiments on controlled benchmarks, reachability graphs, and ontology-derived instances demonstrate that our counterinterpretation-guided synthesis achieves up to 92% optimum coverage within practical resource bounds, outperforming scenario expansion and general abduction while confirming the necessity of transversal-based reasoning over proof-packing heuristics. 1 School of Management, Beijing Institute of Technology yangyukun2005@163.com Introduction Rule-based decisions often require premises that can be inspected, retained, or communicated. A release policy may combine signed test reports and attestations; a knowledge graph may infer relationships from several institutions’ records. Efficient materialization computes conclusions ( Motik et al. 2014 ) , while explanation and provenance expose their dependencies. When a provider becomes unavailable or is removed from an audit, the practical question is whether the retained evidence can still justify the decision. An inclusion-minimal explanation removes unnecessary premises, and a minimum-cost explanation reduces inspection or disclosure cost. Neither protects against withdrawal of its own premises: one cheap support may concentrate the entire justification in a single supplier. Retaining the full knowledge base can preserve alternatives but exceed an audit budget. We therefore select a fixed evidence package before failures occur and allow its successful derivation to change afterward. The quantifier order is evidence selection, universal source withdrawal, and existence of a surviving justification. Recovery uses only the selected records, as required by an archived audit package; it does not depend on later evidence acquisition. Counting proofs does not resolve this problem. Different derivations may reuse a record or depend on services within one failure domain. Conversely, requiring domain-disjoint proofs can reject evidence that survives every admissible withdrawal. Robustness depends on whether failed domains intersect all supports, not on whether supports can be packed without overlap. Example 1 (Release authorization). Authorization requires any two of checks a , b , c a,b,c , whose records depend on domains s A , s B , s C s_{A},s_{B},s_{C} . Retaining all three survives any single-domain withdrawal because any two suffice, yet their support footprints { s A , s B } \{s_{A},s_{B}\} , { s A , s C } \{s_{A},s_{C}\} , and { s B , s C } \{s_{B},s_{C}\} share domains pairwise, precluding disjoint proofs. An alternative attestation d d independently authorizes release at higher cost. Optimal robust certification must navigate both inspection costs and failure dependencies. While why-provenance ( Buneman et al. 2001 ) , semiring provenance ( Green et al. 2007 ) , and circuit representations ( Deutch et al. 2014 ) expose derivation dependencies, they do not select cost-optimal subsets resilient to source loss. Database resilience ( Freire et al. 2015 ) and Datalog deletion causality ( Thapa and Staab 2026 ) analyze answer vulnerability to tuple removals via minimal supports, but do not address ex-ante evidence synthesis under grouped, correlated domain withdrawals. Similarly, abduction-based explanations ( Ignatiev et al. 2019 ) , robust perturbation models ( La Malfa et al. 2021 ) , and lineage-driven fault injection ( Alvaro et al. 2015 ) seek explanations or fault witnesses without synthesizing minimum-cost packages resilient to source loss. We turn this support–transversal principle into a cost-sensitive separation framework specialized for correlated source domains. Our synthesis method alternates an exact weighted hitting-set master with an adversarial oracle. A defeating withdrawal yields a rule-closed counterinterpretation and a positive clause that every robust selection must satisfy. This uses established implicit hitting-set separation ( Saikko et al. 2016 ; Davies and Bacchus 2011 ) , with globally valid record cuts for shared failures. Horn closure handles recursive rules without admitting unsupported cycles as proofs. Our contributions are: (1) a record-level certification objective capturing correlated source failures; (2) a footprint characterization proving why proof packing is incomplete; (3) an exact synthesis algorithm with finite termination and cost optimality guarantees; (4) complexity results showing coNP-complete verification and NP-complete synthesis for fixed budgets; (5) a polynomial flow reduction for independent reachability; and (6) empirical evaluations demonstrating up to 92% optimum coverage and the necessity of cut strengthening over proof packing.
